title: What Ultra Tight Credit Spreads Are Really Telling...
content:
What Ultra Tight Credit Spreads Are Really Telling You
Corporate bond spreads are sitting near their tightest levels since 2007, which on the surface reads as confidence..low defaults, steady growth, plenty of liquidity. Credit markets are basically saying, “We’re comfortable here.”
But that comfort is exactly what should make you pause.
Credit spreads are the price of risk. When they’re wide, investors are nervous and demand compensation. When they’re this ..tight around 100 basis points, investors are saying very little can go wrong. That’s not optimism, that’s pricing perfection.
Why Tight Spreads Aren’t The Same As Safe
The problem with spreads this tight is how little margin for error there is. You’re barely getting paid to take credit risk. A modest slowdown, a hiccup in refinancing, or a small liquidity shock is enough to wipe out the extra yield you’re earning. At wider spreads, you have room to be wrong. Here, you don’t.
There’s also an asymmetry that matters. From these levels, spreads can only tighten a little more. But they can widen a lot, and when they do, it tends to happen fast. That’s why periods of ultra tight spreads often feel calm right before they don’t.
This isn’t about predicting an imminent blow up. Tight spreads can persist for a while. But historically, they show up when confidence is highest, not when risk is lowest. Defaults are a lagging indicator. By the time they rise, spreads have already moved.
How This Can Make Downturns Worse
Cheap credit changes behavior. Companies borrow more, refinance aggressively, stretch balance sheets, and assume funding will always be available. That works fine until conditions shift. When growth slows or rates stay higher for longer, refinancing suddenly becomes harder and more expensive. What could have been a mild slowdown turns sharper because leverage was built at the wrong time.
That’s why tight spreads don’t just fail to protect you..they can actually amplify the next downturn.
My View
I don’t read this chart as everything is fine. I read it as credit is priced as if the cycle can’t turn. That can hold for a while, but it leaves the system fragile. When risk is priced cheaply, small shocks have outsized effects.
In 2007, spreads didn’t warn anyone ahead of time. They told you the market had stopped charging for risk. That’s what this looks like too.

title: US corporate debt is getting worse again after a p...
content:
US corporate debt is getting worse again after a pretty good year in 2024.
 When companies borrow in the bond market, they receive credit ratings, similar to a credit score. 
So far in 2025, about $55 billion of corporate bonds have been pushed down from investment‑grade to junk, the most since 2020. 
Over the same period, only around $10 billion of bonds have been upgraded into investment grade, the weakest upgrade volume in at least six years. 
That means there are roughly 5.5 times more bonds getting worse than getting better. 
In 2024 it was the reverse: there were far more upgrades than downgrades. 
On top of that, roughly $63 billion of bonds are sitting just one step above junk status, up sharply from $37 billion at the end of 2024. 
Think of that as a growing group of companies standing on the edge of a downgrade cliff.
The implications are mainly about risk and borrowing costs. 
When a company is downgraded, especially from investment grade to junk, its bond price usually falls and its yield jumps. 
That means it becomes more expensive for the company to issue new debt or refinance old debt that’s coming due.
 Higher interest costs squeeze profits and cash flow, and if enough firms are in that position, defaults and bankruptcies tend to rise over time. 
This is why a spike in downgrades is often treated as an early warning sign of building stress in corporate balance sheets.
There is also a big impact on large investors. 
Many institutions like pension funds and insurance companies are restricted to owning only investment grade bonds. 
When a bond drops into junk territory, they may be forced to sell. 
Those forced sales can push prices down further and make financing even tougher for the downgraded companies. 
For regular investors who own bond funds, that can show up as more volatility or losses in funds that were assumed to be fairly safe.
At the economy wide level, more downgrades and a larger pile of near‑junk issuers usually mean tighter financial conditions. 
Investors, seeing rising risk, demand higher yields more broadly. 
Higher borrowing costs lead companies to pull back on hiring, investment and buybacks, which can slow economic growth and raise recession odds at the margin.
 It does not mean an immediate crisis, the overall corporate bond market is huge so $55 billion is a warning but it clearly says the direction of travel in credit quality is negative.
US corporate bond downgrades are surging at an alarming pace:
$55 billion of corporate bonds were downgraded from investment-grade to junk status in 2025, the highest since 2020.
At the same time, only $10 billion of upgrades to investment-grade were recorded, the lowest in at least 6 years.
This means downgrade volumes were 5.5 times higher than upgrades, compared to 4.8 times in 2020.
By comparison, in 2024, there were only $4 billion in downgrades and $22 billion in upgrades, meaning upgrades outpaced downgrades by 5.5 times.
Meanwhile, $63 billion of bonds are now on the brink of junk status, up from $37 billion at the end of 2024.
The credit quality of US corporate bonds is deteriorating. 
- 
The Kobeissi Letter

title: No Job Growth Almost Anywhere..A Market That’s Sto...
content:
No Job Growth Almost Anywhere..A Market That’s Stopped Expanding
In November, unemployment was higher than a year ago in 259 of 387 metro areas. That’s roughly two thirds of the country moving in the wrong direction at the same time. When deterioration is that broad, it’s rarely random. Historically, this kind of breadth shows up when the labor market is rolling over, not stabilizing.
What makes this more unsettling is that the core looks worse than the edges. Among the largest metro divisions, the inner engines of big cities..about 85% saw unemployment rise year over year. When the centers start cracking, it usually means the slowdown is no longer local or sector-specific.
The Outliers Show Where The Stress Is Coming From
Take Wildwood..The Villages, Florida, where unemployment jumped 3 full percentage points in a year. This isn’t a tech hub or factory town..it’s retirement and service heavy. Similar stress appears across Florida metros tied to tourism, housing churn, and discretionary spending. That’s typically where downturns surface first, because those jobs disappear quietly and early.
On the other end, places like Kokomo, Indiana, which show sharp unemployment declines, look more like one off rebounds or demographic quirks than broad strength. These wins are usually tied to small labor forces, base effects, or people leaving the workforce..not hiring momentum that spreads.
Then there’s Washington, DC. Its core division saw unemployment rise more than 2 points, while payrolls fell sharply. That matters because federal employment is usually insulated in the data. If DC is weakening even with those protections, the underlying stress is likely worse than what’s being reported.
The Quietest Red Flag Is Almost No Job Growth Anywhere…
Here’s the line that should stop you..only 8 metro areas added jobs year over year. Two lost jobs. The other 377 were essentially unchanged.
That doesn’t mean nothing is happening. It means job growth is so weak and scattered it doesn’t clear statistical noise. In healthy expansions, gains show up clearly across dozens of metros. This looks more like a quiet hiring freeze..firms not firing aggressively, but not adding people either.
Why The Shutdown Likely Made Things Look Better Than They Are
The federal shutdown distorted the data. There was no October household survey, and November’s response rate fell to 64%, with some states below 50%. When response rates collapse, the people most likely to disappear from the sample are those under stress..the unemployed, the marginally attached, people moving or doubling up.
On top of that, statistical weighting had to be shifted forward because October was missing. That mechanically pulls older labor conditions into the present. In plain terms, the process smooths weakness rather than exaggerating it.
Federal workers were counted as employed even if furloughed, while contractors who didn’t get paid weren’t. That asymmetry means federal heavy areas likely looked better on paper than they felt in reality.
Why Unemployment Is Rising While Payrolls Look Flat
Unemployment comes from a household survey tracking people where they live. Payrolls come from an establishment survey tracking jobs where they’re located. When unemployment rises broadly while payrolls barely move, it often means hours are being cut before headcount, multiple jobholding is masking stress, and hiring has stalled even if layoffs haven’t surged.
That’s how downturns usually begin. The national unemployment rate is one of the last things to break.
My View
Strip away the smoothing and shutdown distortions, and this doesn’t look like a healthy labor market pausing..it looks like quiet, widespread weakening, stalled job growth, and data lagging reality.
That’s what the early stage of a labor downturn looks like..subtle, broad, and easy to ignore until it isn’t.

Representative Lisa McClain's husband bought xAI stock on December 15, 2025. 
A week later, the Pentagon announced it was using xAI's technology. 
Within two weeks, xAI got access to classified military networks. 
When asked if this was insider trading, McClain essentially said: "If it was, we would've bought way more."​
This is why every politician needs to be completely banned from trading stocks while in office. Period.
Congress passed a law in 2012 called the STOCK Act that's supposed to stop politicians from trading on insider information.
Sounds good, right? It's completely useless.​
Nobody has ever been prosecuted under it. 
The penalty for breaking it is $200 basically nothing. In 2020 and 2021, at least 63 members of Congress violated it by not reporting their trades on time. 
Some were years late. Nothing happened to them.​
The law is full of holes. Politicians can claim they didn't use insider information they just made a smart investment. 
They can have their wife trade instead. 
They can disclose trades months late with almost no punishment. It's regulation that doesn't regulate anything.​
Trying to regulate congressional stock trading doesn't work. 
You can't prove what information a politician had or what they knew. 
You can't enforce rules when the penalties mean nothing. 
The only solution that actually works is a complete ban.
If politicians can't own stocks, they have no reason to pass laws that help certain companies over others. 
They make decisions based on what's best for their voters, not what's best for their stock portfolio.​
It's that simple.
This already works for federal employees. 
About 7,000 career government workers can't trade individual stocks. 
If it's good enough for them, why isn't it good enough for Congress?​
Eighty-six percent of Americans want to ban congressional stock trading. 
That's Republicans, Democrats, and independents all agreeing. 
That never happens. When it does, Congress should listen.​
Studies show that when people see politicians making money off their position, they stop trusting the government. 
A complete ban fixes this by removing the conflict of interest entirely.​
Congress should pass a law that says, members of Congress, the President, and senior government officials cannot own individual stocks. 
They have six months to sell what they already own or put it in accounts they can't control. 
Their spouses and kids can't trade either. That's it. Done.

title: AI Didn’t Start the Fire It Just Made the Cuts Eas...
content:
AI Didn’t Start the Fire It Just Made the Cuts Easier to Explain
This chart pretty much settles the debate. Hiring in the most AI exposed jobs started rolling over before ChatGPT even existed. So AI can’t be the original cause. The slowdown was already in motion. What changed wasn’t technology, it was the economic environment.
Once money stopped being cheap, the math changed everywhere
What Actually Shifted
From 2020 through early 2022, companies hired like growth was guaranteed. Capital was easy, demand looked endless, and nobody got punished for being early or excessive. Headcount was treated as an option on future growth.
Then rates rose. Liquidity tightened. Valuations reset. Boards stopped asking “How fast can we grow?” and started asking “What do we really need to keep margins intact?”
That’s when hiring freezes show up first. Layoffs always come later. They’re the lagging admission that the world didn’t turn out the way the org chart assumed.
Why AI Became The Explanation 
Blaming the economy sounds like failure. Blaming AI sounds strategic.
Saying “demand slowed and our cost base is too big” rattles investors. Saying “we’re restructuring for the AI era” sounds proactive, forward looking, even inevitable. Same outcome, very different story.
There’s also a capital allocation angle. AI isn’t free. Compute, infrastructure, data, security..it all costs real money. If you’re committing to that spend, the easiest way to fund it is by cutting operating expenses. Headcount is the fastest lever.
So AI becomes the narrative wrapper for a decision that was already economically forced.
What I Think Is Really Driving Layoffs
At the core, this isn’t about machines replacing people overnight. It’s about four very human dynamics..
First, the delayed impact of higher rates. Expensive capital doesn’t just hit consumers. It raises hurdle rates inside companies. Projects get cut. Teams stop expanding. Nice to have roles suddenly need to justify themselves.
Second, pandemic overbuild. A lot of firms staffed for 2021 conditions that were never sustainable. When demand normalized, the excess became obvious.
Third, the investor regime changed. Growth at any cost stopped being rewarded. Cash flow, margins, and discipline took its place. Layoffs are the fastest way to signal that shift.
Fourth, internal reprioritization. Many cuts aren’t about shrinking the company, they’re about shrinking legacy work to fund what leadership thinks matters next. AI just happens to be the bucket everything gets poured into.
Where AI Actually Is Having An Impact
AI isn’t irrelevant, it’s just not the spark.
Its real effect right now is quieter: fewer new job postings, slower backfills, tighter junior pipelines, and roles being compressed rather than wiped out. One person with better tools replaces 1.2 people, not five. That adds up over time, but it doesn’t explain the timing in the data.
The pressure shows up first in hiring. Layoffs are the headline, but suppressed hiring is the real structural shift.
What This Means Going Forward
Even if the economy improves, don’t expect hiring to snap back the way it used to especially in white collar, AI adjacent work. Companies have learned they can run leaner, and the tools keep improving.
The cycle and the cost of capital caused the layoffs. AI is accelerating the reshuffle and making the story easier to tell.
AI didn’t start the fire. It just became the most convenient explanation for why the house needed to be reworked once the interest rate doubled.

title: When Commodities Lead But Energy Doesn’t, the Cycl...
content:
When Commodities Lead But Energy Doesn’t, the Cycle Is Talking
When the broader commodity complex is moving higher and energy stocks aren’t, that’s not noise..it’s a signal. Historically, energy is usually the most sensitive part of the commodity trade. When it lags this badly late in the cycle, it tells you the market isn’t rejecting commodities, it’s pricing in weaker growth and singling out oil and gas as the pressure valve.
That’s not just about prices. It’s about expectations for demand in a slowing world.
Why Energy Keeps Getting Left Behind
On the surface, the reasons are familiar. Oil in the high $50s fits neatly into a downturn narrative. Oversupply stories get louder, demand fears dominate, and every soft macro print reinforces the idea that energy will be the first thing hit when growth rolls over.
But there’s a deeper layer. In a late cycle environment, energy gets mentally reclassified. It’s treated less like a growth asset and more like a run off business. Investors assume production discipline means stagnation, and they assume the energy transition caps upside just as demand risks are rising. In a downturn, that combination is enough to keep capital on the sidelines.
So even when energy companies are generating cash, buying back shares, and improving balance sheets, the market shrugs. It doesn’t line up with the slowing global economy story people want to believe.
What This Actually Means In A Downturn
This isn’t a call that oil is about to rip higher into a recession. It’s about asymmetry.
Commodity equities outside of energy are increasingly priced around long term scarcity, geopolitics, and underinvestment. Energy equities, by contrast, are priced as if demand destruction is inevitable and supply will always show up on time. In a global downturn, those assumptions feel comfortable until they collide with reality.
Downturns suppress demand, but they also suppress investment. Capex gets cut, projects get delayed, labor leaves the sector, and spare capacity quietly erodes. When growth stabilizes..not booms, just stabilizes the energy market often finds itself tighter than expected.
That’s the tension sitting in this chart.
My View
Energy can stay frustrating longer than people expect, especially if the global slowdown deepens. In that scenario, the sector can keep wearing the dead money label while investors crowd into other parts of the commodity complex that feel more structural or strategic.
But that same downturn is what sets up the next phase. If oil simply doesn’t collapse and if it holds a floor while investment continues to lag the disconnect starts to matter. Cash flows persist. Buybacks quietly compound. And when growth bottoms, energy is no longer priced for the world it’s actually entering.
Energy doesn’t need a roaring expansion to work. In many cycles, it works best coming out of the downturn, not going into it.
The Line That Matters
If a global recession drives oil materially lower and keeps it there, this divergence can last. Full stop.
But if the downturn is shallow, uneven, or followed by stabilization, this chart looks less like energy is dead and more like energy is being discounted as if the downturn never ends and markets rarely price that correctly for very long.

title: Why the Scariest Signal Right Now Is How Calm Ever...
content:
Why the Scariest Signal Right Now Is How Calm Everything Feels
If the Treasury market were genuinely panicking about threats to Fed independence, you wouldn’t have to squint to see it. Yields would be jumping around. Volatility would be rising. Investors would be paying up for protection.
Instead, MOVE is sitting near multi year lows. That’s not fear. That’s the bond market basically saying: this isn’t changing the near term path.
Why Volatility Is Collapsing Anyway
This isn’t about optimism. It’s about predictability.
Right now the market sees a narrow range of outcomes..growth cooling, inflation easing, and a central bank that’s cautious and unlikely to shock anyone. When the future feels boxed in like that, there’s no reason to chase hedges. Volatility fades because the path feels known, not because risks are gone.
There’s also an uncomfortable wrinkle here. Political pressure can actually reduce perceived upside risk in yields if investors think it ultimately leads to easier policy. Messy headlines don’t always translate into higher volatility..sometimes they do the opposite.
So low MOVE isn’t the market saying everything’s fine. It’s saying, we know roughly how this plays out.
What This Really Tells You
The bond market is pricing a managed slowdown, not a regime break.
It’s not bracing for chaos, it’s settling into a grind.
That can be deceptive. When volatility collapses this much, it usually means expectations have converged. Everyone is leaning the same way, comfortable with the same story. And that’s when markets tend to be most vulnerable to surprises.
The Risk Isn’t Panic It’s Comfort
Low volatility doesn’t mean safety. It means consensus.
And consensus, especially late in the cycle, has a habit of cracking not because people were scared but because they were too sure they didn’t need to be.

content:
What Actually Stood Out In This H.4.1
If you read this like a normal person instead of a policy document, the story is where liquidity has quietly moved, and just as important, where the Fed is choosing not to apply pressure.
Nothing jumps off the page. That’s intentional. Stability is the message.
The Headline Numbers (and why they matter)
A few things stand out once you slow down and look at the mix..
•   Total Fed assets rose about $8B week over week, even though they’re still down roughly $252B year over year.
On its own, that weekly increase looks like noise. It stops being noise when you see what drove it.
•   Treasury holdings rose about $13.6B WoW, taking total Treasuries to roughly $4.24T.
Almost all of that came from Treasury bills (+$14.0B WoW), while notes and bonds were basically unchanged.
That choice matters. Bills are short duration, highly liquid, and easy to roll. This isn’t QE but it is the Fed keeping things flexible and minimizing disruption.
QT Is Still Happening … Just With Guardrails 
The Fed can keep QT technically on while running it in a way that avoids stress.
•   MBS holdings were flat on the week at $2.039T, even though they’re still down about $194B year over year.
•   In a high rate environment, prepayments slow, so runoff naturally slows. That part is normal.
•   The effect, though, is that housing isn’t providing much passive tightening anymore.
So QT continues on paper, but one of the most economically sensitive channels isn’t really doing the heavy lifting right now.
Liquidity Didn’t Grow It Relocated 
This is where the plumbing tells the real story..
•   Reserve balances jumped about $53B WoW to $3.05
•   Reverse repo (RRP) usage fell roughly $30B WoW, into the low $320B range
•   Treasury General Account (TGA) dropped about $17B WoW
That explains why markets feel calmer. Liquidity didn’t suddenly appear, it shifted..
•   out of places that park or absorb liquidity (RRP, TGA),
•   into bank reserves, where it actually supports market functioning.
That’s why volatility feels suppressed even though the macro backdrop hasn’t magically improved.
The quiet anomaly worth noting..
•   Repo operations fell by roughly $20B WoW, basically to zero
That doesn’t scream crisis. It could be technical or timing related. But it’s a reminder that weekly calm can hide real movement underneath. The surface can look smooth while the pipes are still adjusting.
My View
This doesn’t look like a Fed that’s panicking. It looks like a Fed that’s tightening carefully without letting it bite too hard.
They’re..
•   allowing the balance sheet to drift lower over time,
•   leaning toward short duration Treasuries,
•   tolerating slower MBS runoff
•   and letting reserves rebuild as RRP drains.
That’s not easing. But it’s not aggressive tightening either. It’s risk control.
What I’d Watch Next
If this pattern keeps going..
•   reserves keep rising,
•   RRP keeps drifting lower,
•   and bills keep growing faster than longer dated runoff,
markets will increasingly interpret this as stealth accommodation, regardless of how carefully the Fed words it.
So the real question isn’t is QT still on? 
It’s whether QT is being reshaped into something that doesn’t break the system and whether that’s because conditions are genuinely healthy, or because they’re more fragile than the headlines want to admit.

title: PPI Report Reality Check And Why November’s Calm H...
content:
PPI Report Reality Check And Why November’s Calm Headline Is Hiding Growing Economic Strain
The November PPI report doesn’t look dramatic. Headline final demand prices rose 0.2% month over month. If you stop there, it’s easy to conclude inflation is contained and the system is behaving.
But that headline hides where the pressure actually is.
What’s Driving The Number
Most of the move came from goods prices, which jumped 0.9% the biggest monthly increase in nearly two years. A large chunk of that was energy. Final demand energy prices rose 4.6%, with gasoline up more than 10% in a single month. That alone explains a meaningful share of the headline increase.
Meanwhile, services prices were flat. That divergence matters. It tells you this wasn’t broad based pricing power across the economy. it was a cost shock hitting specific inputs.
Strip out food, energy, and trade services, and core PPI was up 0.2% on the month and 3.5% year over year. That’s still elevated, but it’s not accelerating. It’s steady pressure, not runaway inflation.
Margins Are Getting Squeezed
The most important part of this report isn’t the headline. It’s trade services.
Wholesale and retail margins fell 0.8% in November, the largest drop since April. That means businesses weren’t able to pass higher costs through cleanly. They absorbed them.
This is how stress usually shows up before it hits growth or jobs. Not through collapsing demand, but through thinner margins. Companies discount. They compete harder. They protect volume instead of profit.
You can have inflation still running around 3% year over year and still have an economy that’s quietly losing pricing power.
Upstream vs. Downstream Tells the Same Story
Intermediate demand prices rose 0.3%, with processed goods up 0.6% and unprocessed goods up 0.4%. Energy again did most of the work. On a year over year basis, the earliest stage of production is still running hot..Stage 1 prices are up 3.7%, the fastest pace since early 2023.
That means costs are still moving through the pipeline.
But downstream, margins are narrowing. That gap of rising inputs, contested pricing is classic late cycle behavior.
What This Is (And Isn’t)
Producer prices are still rising year over year. Demand hasn’t collapsed. But it’s also not confirming a clean disinflation narrative.
Instead, it shows an economy where…
•   input costs can still spike suddenly,
•   consumers are more price sensitive,
•   and businesses are absorbing volatility rather than passing it on.
That’s not a healthy expansion phase. It’s a balancing act.
My View
The PPI isn’t telling you inflation is back. It’s telling you inflation is uneven, and the burden of adjustment is shifting onto corporate margins.
That’s usually how the cycle turns. Not with a crash in prices, but with companies losing room to maneuver. When margins compress long enough, hiring slows, capex gets cautious, and growth cools without a headline moment.
This print looks calm on the surface. Underneath, it’s signaling an economy that’s still under pressure..just in subtler, more uncomfortable ways.

title: January 2026 Beige Book Looks Stable On The Surfac...
content:
January 2026 Beige Book Looks Stable On The Surface But Fragile Underneath
8 of 12 districts reported “slight to modest” growth, 3 were flat, and only 1 saw a modest decline. That’s technically an improvement from recent cycles where “little change” dominated. But the details tell a more conditional story.  
Where The Growth Is Coming From
Most of the momentum came from holiday related consumer spending, and even that was uneven..
•   Spending was strongest among higher income households, especially on luxury goods, travel, and experiences.
•   Low and moderate income consumers were increasingly price sensitive, hesitating on nonessential purchases.
•   Auto sales were flat to down across most districts.
•   Manufacturing was split: 5 districts expanding, 6 contracting.
That’s not broad based strength. It’s a narrow pocket of resilience.
Labor Is Stable, but Defensive
Employment was described as “mostly unchanged”..
•   8 of 12 districts reported no net hiring growth.
•   When firms hired, it was mostly to backfill, not expand.
•   Multiple districts reported increased use of temporary workers “to stay flexible in uncertain times.”
•   Wage growth was moderate and back to pre pandemic norms, not accelerating.
One concrete data point cuts through the language: in Minneapolis, job postings fell 18% year over year. That’s not collapse..but it’s cooling.
Prices and Tariffs And The Margin Squeeze
Prices were said to be rising at a moderate pace, but tariffs were a consistent pressure across districts..
•   Firms that had been absorbing tariff costs are now passing them through as pre tariff inventories run out.
•   At the same time, retailers and restaurants are reluctant to raise prices because customers are price sensitive.
•   Energy and insurance costs were repeatedly cited as margin stressors.
This is the key tension..costs are rising faster than many businesses can pass them on.
Examples from districts..
•   Boston reported credit card processing fees up to 4%, with some merchants eating the cost.
•   St. Louis and Cleveland noted restaurants unable to pass costs along, leading to financial strain.
•   Dallas data showed manufacturing input costs averaged 5.5% in 2025, while selling prices rose only 2.3%.
That gap is where slowdowns usually start.
Consumers: K Shaped and Cautious
Across districts, the same pattern showed up..
•   Higher income consumers kept spending.
•   Middle and lower income households were trading down, comparing prices, and cutting discretionary spending.
•   In Cleveland, nearly 70% of low income workers said expenses rose, about half said income didn’t cover costs, and 45% planned to look for new jobs.
That’s pressure, not confidence.
My View
The Beige Book isn’t describing a confident expansion. It’s an economy that’s still moving, but on thinner margins and narrower demand.
The risk here isn’t a sudden break. It’s a grind..
•   rising input costs,
•   delayed price pass through,
•   margin compression,
•   cautious hiring,
•   and increasingly selective consumers.
That’s how growth slows quietly without a headline moment and the Beige Book, despite its calm tone, is already sketching that outline.
Read about economic conditions in Reserve Bank Districts in the #BeigeBook: https://t.co/e3QNq5khGx (1/2) https://t.co/2GCe77DuH9 
- 
Federal Reserve
